turns.user: Can a landlord evict a tenant without giving any notice in India?
turns.answer:
No, a landlord generally cannot evict a tenant without giving notice in India. The law specifies notice periods for terminating leases, especially when there is no written contract or local usage to the contrary [1].

According to Section 106 of The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, if there is no contract, local law, or usage stating otherwise, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes is considered a year-to-year lease, which can be ended by either the landlord or tenant with six months' notice [1]. For any other purpose, a lease of immovable property is considered a month-to-month lease, terminable by either the landlord or tenant with fifteen days' notice [1]. The period of notice begins from the date the notice is received [1]. A notice is not invalid just because the period mentioned in it is shorter than the specified period, as long as a suit or proceeding is filed after the specified period has expired [1]. Every notice must be in writing, signed by or on behalf of the person giving it, and sent by post, or delivered personally to the party or a family member/servant at their residence, or affixed to a visible part of the property if personal delivery is not practical [1].

turns.user: Is an employee entitled to gratuity if they resign before completing 5 years?
turns.answer:
No, an employee is generally not entitled to gratuity if they resign before completing five years of continuous service, according to The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 [1].

Gratuity is payable to an employee upon termination of employment after they have rendered continuous service for not less than five years [1]. This includes termination due to superannuation, retirement, or resignation [1]. However, the requirement of completing five years of continuous service is not necessary if the termination of employment is due to death or disablement [1]. "Continuous service" means continuous service as defined in Section 2-A of the Act [4].

If there is a dispute regarding the amount of gratuity, or who is entitled to it, the employer or employee or any other person can apply to the controlling authority to decide the dispute [2]. The controlling authority will conduct an inquiry and direct the employer to pay the determined amount [2]. If the employer does not pay the gratuity within thirty days from the date it becomes payable, they must pay simple interest [2]. If the gratuity is not paid within the prescribed time, the controlling authority can issue a certificate to the Collector, who will recover the amount with compound interest as arrears of land revenue [3].

General background (not from the retrieved sources): Gratuity is a lump sum payment made by an employer to an employee as a token of appreciation for services rendered. It is one of the many retirement benefits offered to employees in India.

Note: several central labour laws, including the Payment of Wages Act, the Minimum Wages Act, the Payment of Gratuity Act and the Industrial Disputes Act, have been consolidated into the Code on Wages, the Code on Social Security, the Industrial Relations Code and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code. turns.user: I bought a defective product online and the company refuses to replace it. What should I do?
turns.answer:
If you have bought a defective product online and the company refuses to replace it, you can file a complaint under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. A "complaint" means a written allegation made by a complainant to get relief under this Act [2].

Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
*   A "complainant" can be a consumer, a voluntary consumer association, the Central or State Government, the Central Authority, or one or more consumers with the same interest [2]. In case of a consumer's death, their legal heir or representative can be the complainant, and for a minor consumer, their parent or legal guardian can complain [2].
*   A "complaint" can be made if a trader or service provider has adopted an unfair contract, unfair trade practice, or restrictive trade practice [2]. It also covers situations where goods bought suffer from defects, or services hired suffer from deficiencies [2]. Charging a price in excess of the fixed or displayed price is also grounds for a complaint [2]. Refusing to take back or withdraw defective goods or discontinue deficient services and refund the money within the stipulated period (or 30 days if no period is stipulated) is also a reason for a complaint [2].
*   The Central Authority, established under Section 10 of the Act, has an Investigation Wing headed by a Director-General to conduct inquiries or investigations as directed by the Central Authority [1]. The Central Government appoints the Director-General and other officers who have experience in investigation [1]. These officers exercise their powers under the general control and supervision of the Director-General [1]. The Director-General can delegate powers to other officers for inquiries or investigations [1]. The inquiries or investigations made by the Director-General are submitted to the Central Authority [1].
*   The Central Government provides the Central Authority with the necessary officers and employees for its functions [4]. The Central Authority can also engage experts and professionals with special knowledge in areas like consumer rights, law, and product safety to assist it [4].
*   A Central Consumer Protection Council, known as the Central Council, is established by the Central Government [5]. This Central Council is an advisory council, chaired by the Minister-in-charge of the Department of Consumer Affairs [5].
*   Proceedings of the Central Authority are not invalid just because of a vacancy, a defect in its constitution, a defect in the appointment of a Chief Commissioner or Commissioner, or an irregularity in procedure that does not affect the case's merits [3].

General background (not from the retrieved sources):
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 aims to protect the interests of consumers and provides mechanisms for redressal of consumer grievances.

cases.final_answer:
If you have bought a defective product online and the company refuses to replace it, you can file a complaint under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. A "complaint" means a written allegation made by a complainant to get relief under this Act [2].

Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
*   A "complainant" can be a consumer, a voluntary consumer association, the Central or State Government, the Central Authority, or one or more consumers with the same interest [2]. In case of a consumer's death, their legal heir or representative can be the complainant, and for a minor consumer, their parent or legal guardian can complain [2].
*   A "complaint" can be made if a trader or service provider has adopted an unfair contract, unfair trade practice, or restrictive trade practice [2]. It also covers situations where goods bought suffer from defects, or services hired suffer from deficiencies [2]. Charging a price in excess of the fixed or displayed price is also grounds for a complaint [2]. Refusing to take back or withdraw defective goods or discontinue deficient services and refund the money within the stipulated period (or 30 days if no period is stipulated) is also a reason for a complaint [2].
*   The Central Authority, established under Section 10 of the Act, has an Investigation Wing headed by a Director-General to conduct inquiries or investigations as directed by the Central Authority [1]. The Central Government appoints the Director-General and other officers who have experience in investigation [1]. These officers exercise their powers under the general control and supervision of the Director-General [1]. The Director-General can delegate powers to other officers for inquiries or investigations [1]. The inquiries or investigations made by the Director-General are submitted to the Central Authority [1].
*   The Central Government provides the Central Authority with the necessary officers and employees for its functions [4]. The Central Authority can also engage experts and professionals with special knowledge in areas like consumer rights, law, and product safety to assist it [4].
*   A Central Consumer Protection Council, known as the Central Council, is established by the Central Government [5]. This Central Council is an advisory council, chaired by the Minister-in-charge of the Department of Consumer Affairs [5].
*   Proceedings of the Central Authority are not invalid just because of a vacancy, a defect in its constitution, a defect in the appointment of a Chief Commissioner or Commissioner, or an irregularity in procedure that does not affect the case's merits [3].
